pr_body:
Closes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/60866

A quick benchmark:
```csharp
[Benchmark]
public int IndexOf_Still() =>
    "Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still...".AsSpan().IndexOf("still");

[Benchmark]
public int LastIndexOf_Sherlock() =>
    "Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still...".AsSpan().LastIndexOf("sat");

[Benchmark]
public bool Contains_HtmlTag() =>
    "<html>Text</html>".Contains("</html>");

[Benchmark]
public int IndexOf_Cmake() => 
    GlobalJson.AsSpan().IndexOf("\"cmake\"");


static readonly string GlobalJson = File.ReadAllText(@"C:\prj\runtime\global.json");
```
|               Method |                  Toolchain |       Mean |     Error |    StdDev | Ratio |
|--------------------- |--------------------------- |-----------:|----------:|----------:|------:|
|        IndexOf_Still | Core_Root_Base\corerun.exe |  34.543 ns | 0.0262 ns | 0.0219 ns |  1.00 |
|        IndexOf_Still | Core_Root_EGOR\corerun.exe |   9.651 ns | 0.0245 ns | 0.0229 ns |  0.28 |
|                      |                            |            |           |           |       |
| LastIndexOf_Sherlock | Core_Root_Base\corerun.exe |  32.467 ns | 0.0313 ns | 0.0278 ns |  1.00 |
| LastIndexOf_Sherlock | Core_Root_EGOR\corerun.exe |  10.252 ns | 0.0399 ns | 0.0373 ns |  0.32 |
|                      |                            |            |           |           |       |
|     Contains_HtmlTag | Core_Root_Base\corerun.exe |  12.484 ns | 0.0041 ns | 0.0037 ns |  1.00 |
|     Contains_HtmlTag | Core_Root_EGOR\corerun.exe |   8.579 ns | 0.0044 ns | 0.0039 ns |  0.69 |
|                      |                            |            |           |           |       |
|        IndexOf_Cmake | Core_Root_Base\corerun.exe | 130.526 ns | 0.0912 ns | 0.0712 ns |  1.00 |
|        IndexOf_Cmake | Core_Root_EGOR\corerun.exe |  20.411 ns | 0.0110 ns | 0.0092 ns |  0.16 |


The algorithm is based on http://0x80.pl/articles/simd-strfind.html#algorithm-1-generic-simd
where for this specific word "walking" we populate two 128/256bit vectors: `<w,w,w,w,w...w>` and `<g,g,g,g,g...g>` and apply them to a current chunk of the text with an offset (distance between `w` and `g` in that word). 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/523221/148053125-5032749c-6dcf-49f1-9f3b-155c6be457f6.png)

While the currently used algorithm just does `IndexOf(text, 'w')` + `SequenceEquals` for each substring starting with `w` it finds.

TODO:
- [x] Add Arm64 impl
- [x] IndexOf (byte)
- [x] IndexOf (char)
- [x] LastIndexOf (byte)
- [x] LastIndexOf (char)
- [x] Implement "find last unique char" if last == first
- [x] Benchmarks for various inputs, not just the worst cases for the currently used algorithm
- [x] Copyrights
- [x] Optional: support OrdinalIgnoreCase (done separately)

Nice! The worst case for this algorithm is a small string + value that doesn't exist in it (its first character), e.g.:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/523221/147987132-0e48cc05-f049-4712-9801-c5b2d64ddf53.png)

for larger strings (once AVX path is kicked in) the regression disappears.

As a possible solution we can use the old one till the first hit (`IndexOf(firstChar)`) and switch to the new algorithm after. So in cases like ^ we only will do a single IndexOf that won't find anything.

At the same time, the worst case for the baseline algorithm is when it has to stop every character:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/523221/148045346-08fed119-fe20-406d-b912-1d6497e675c8.png)

(the new one is 20x faster)

For better performance (with potential trade-offs) we can do more here:
1) Align data in the SIMD loop using pointer arithmetics (single-byte/char IndexOf does it) - quite verbose
2) Use `nint/nuint` everywhere to avoid redundant sign/zero extensions where `int` is currently used - but it's a more global task for the whole SpanHelpers
3) Partially inline "SequenceCompare" inside IndexOf/LastIndexOf to handle small-sized values
4) I noticed that in some cases my SIMD loops aren't aligned in JIT, e.g.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/523221/148702088-726af7fe-0caf-43c1-9b59-b9634b1d985d.png)

Benchmarks: https://gist.github.com/EgorBo/baef36b2fb0b31d99464257f9d001e6c (I run them with `--coreRun ... --warmupCount 30` args because otherwise I feel like some methods are randomly not promoted to tier1 and the results are not stable).

https://gist.github.com/EgorBo/29ccb19fd8c9adc05c8fcd37a5415549

There are some cases where the new algorithm is slower e.g. where we don't even meet the first character = it means we do the second data load + CompareEquals + And in vain. I tried to modify the algorithm to do single-char/byte IndexOf and then switch to the new one after first "false positive" match but it goes with its own regressions. Overall, it's better IMO. issue_context.title: Improve vectorization of MemoryExtensions.IndexOf(..., span)
issue_context.body:
Today `MemoryExtensions.IndexOf(..., ReadOnlySpan<char>)` is implemented essentially as a loop around an IndexOf for the first character in the pattern and then a SequenceEqual at that position for that pattern:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/c742923991c68808d55a9f7cfcd7796644fea44f/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/SpanHelpers.Char.cs#L17-L57
This is good but not great.  In particular it ends up breaking out of the vectorized search loop potentially much more frequently than is necessary and paying the startup overhead for the SequenceEqual each time.

There are better options.  For example, the simple algorithm described in [Algorithm 1: Generic SIMD](http://0x80.pl/articles/simd-strfind.html#algorithm-1-generic-simd) searches concurrently for two characters rather than just one, which makes it much less likely to break out of the vectorized loop to early (this is what the Rust sliceslice crate uses; it's also what the Rust memchr crate uses (which is what's now used by its regex engine), though that memchr doesn't just use the first and last characters but instead picks two characters expected to have the lowest frequency of occurrence).

We could also special-case various sizes.  The aforementioned memchr, for example,  uses Rabin-Karp for small input strings and Two-Way for larger search strings. 

cc: @tannergooding, @GrabYourPitchforks
